title: Common temperate plants share a growth optimum near 26 °C

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Common temperate plants share a growth optimum near 26 °C

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: The optimum temperature for growth is much the same, about 26 °C, for the common plants of temperate climates, and considerably higher for plants of warmer regions such as melon and maize.

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. III: The Rate of Growth

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: this optimum temperature is very much the same for all the common plants of our own climate which have as yet been studied; in them it is somewhere about 26° C. (or say 77° F.), or about the temperature of a warm summer’s day

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci On Growth and Form claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: D’Arcy Wentworth Thompson, On Growth and Form (1st ed., Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1917), Chapter III, “The Rate of Growth”; topic “Effect of temperature”. Scope: temperate and warm-climate plants (root and shoot elongation)

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on thompson1917-ch03-20: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.65

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The optimum and group contrast are directly measurable, but no single open resource appears to contain standardized full response curves for the stated species scope. Existing public studies permit a subset test after harmonization.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: For each species, fit root or shoot elongation across experimental temperatures and estimate the temperature of maximum growth, then compare temperate plants with maize, melon and other warm-climate plants. Broad dispersion among temperate optima or no warmer-climate shift would refute the claim.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Temperature-response experiments are scattered and use different endpoints.

TRY does not directly provide complete temperature-response curves for all species.

Optima depend on developmental stage, organ and acclimation.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
discriminating power: 0.8
analysis feasibility: 0.6
data adequacy: 0.4
operationalizability: 0.9
data existence: 0.55

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: An optimum temperature is a standard parameter of a growth-response curve, and the numerical contrast between about 26°C and a higher warm-climate optimum is discriminating. The curves themselves are spread through experimental papers rather than collected as one open file, and what is well measured is a subset of crops, not the common plants of temperate climates. Compiling that subset is feasible and would resolve only part of the stated scope.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: From growth rate versus temperature, estimate the optimum for common temperate plants and for melon and maize. A shared temperate optimum near 26°C, and a higher optimum for melon and maize, would support the claim. A wide scatter of temperate optima, or no elevation for the warm-climate species, would refute it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Temperate crops are heavily over-represented relative to the common wild flora.

Optimum curves are scattered by species, organ (root versus shoot), and protocol.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
data existence: 0.45
data adequacy: 0.45
analysis feasibility: 0.5
discriminating power: 0.7
operationalizability: 0.85
